q: The first stone Manila Cathedral (1592) and the third cathedral (1614) were both destroyed by what?
n: The second cathedral fell to an earthquake in 1600 and the third to another earthquake in 1645.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Manila Metropolitan Cathedral

q: Antipolo Church was declared by the bishops as the National Shrine of which image?
o: Our Lady of Peace and Good Voyage
Our Lady of the Holy Rosary of La Naval
n: Antipolo is the National Shrine of Our Lady of Peace and Good Voyage (Nuestra Señora de Paz y Buen Viaje).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Antipolo Church

q: At Barasoain, the top pediment is set off by upper side walls that curve inward. That feature belongs to which style?
n: That pediment is the Baroque feature of Barasoain.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Barasoain Church

q: The seventh Manila Cathedral was constructed during which years?
n: The seventh cathedral was built from 1870 to 1879. 1654–1671 is the fourth, and 1954–1958 the present one.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Manila Metropolitan Cathedral

q: Barasoain Church in Bulacan, first built by Augustinian priests in 1859, combines which styles?
n: Barasoain is a combination of Romanesque and Renaissance, with a Baroque crowning pediment.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Barasoain Church

q: What is Las Piñas Church famous for housing?
o: The oldest Marian icon in the country
The image of the Black Nazarene
n: Las Piñas Church houses the famous Bamboo Organ and has an Early Renaissance façade. The Black Nazarene is at Quiapo.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Bamboo Church

q: In 1581, Manila's first bishop built a cathedral of nipa, wood, and bamboo. Who was he?
n: Domingo de Salazar, the first bishop of Manila, built it; it was consecrated December 21, 1581 and destroyed by fire in 1583.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Manila Metropolitan Cathedral

q: The Bamboo Church in Las Piñas was first constructed by whom, and who later reconstructed it?
o: Fr. Juan de Salazar; Juan Nakpil
Fr. Diego Cera; architect Francisco Mañosa
Fr. Juan de Torres; Fernando Ocampo
n: Fr. Diego Cera, an Augustinian Recollect, built the stone church of Las Piñas from 1797 and its famous organ from 1816. Architect Francisco Mañosa later led its reconstruction.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Bamboo Church

q: In 1750, the fourth Manila Cathedral received a media naranja dome at the crossing. What does 'media naranja' mean, and who added it?
o: 'Half orange'; Florentine friar Juan de Uguccioni
n: Media naranja means 'half orange'; the Florentine friar Juan de Uguccioni added the dome and a transept.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Manila Metropolitan Cathedral

q: What happened to the belfry of Our Lady of Manaoag Church in Pangasinan in 1880?
o: It was burned during the revolution
The church demolished it because of cracks caused by an earthquake
n: In 1880 the Dominican church demolished the belfry because of earthquake cracks; the church was completed in 1932.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Our Lady of Manaoag

q: Which church in Bohol has more religious paintings on its walls and ceiling than any other?
n: Loboc Church, built by Fr. Juan de Torres, has the most religious murals. Baclayon's distinction is being the oldest stone church.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Loboc Church

q: Antipolo Church in Rizal was begun by whom, and in what year?
n: Fr. Juan de Salazar began Antipolo Church in 1630. Fr. Juan de Torres is tied to Baclayon and Loboc in Bohol.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Antipolo Church

q: After the 1880 earthquake toppled its bell tower, until what year did Manila Cathedral remain towerless?
n: The cathedral stayed towerless until 1958, when the present cathedral was completed.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Manila Metropolitan Cathedral

q: What is the plan of Antipolo Church?
o: A Latin cross with twin towers
A round plan under one great dome, entered by three main doors
A long rectangle with side chapels
n: Antipolo has a circular plan under a huge dome with three main entrances and Gothic influence on the façade.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Antipolo Church

q: Who built Baclayon Church, and in what style?
o: Fathers de Torres and Sanchez; plain Early Decorated lines
n: Fr. Juan de Torres and Fr. Gabriel Sanchez built Baclayon in 1595, with the simple lines of Early Decorated style.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Baclayon Church

q: Our Lady of Manaoag Church was first built by which order, and when was the church completed?
n: The Dominicans first built Manaoag, and the church was completed in 1932.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Our Lady of Manaoag

q: The present Manila Cathedral (1954–1958) was built under Cardinal Rufino Jiao Santos and supervised by which Filipino architect?
n: Fernando H. Ocampo supervised the present cathedral. Zaragoza designed the current Santo Domingo Church.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Manila Metropolitan Cathedral

q: On Barasoain Church's façade, which element shows the Renaissance?
o: Recessed door jambs with concentric arches
Fluted flat pilasters relieving the walls
A crowning pediment with sweeping concave lines
n: Fluted flat pilasters are the Renaissance element. Recessed jambs with concentric arches are Romanesque, and the concave pediment is Baroque.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Barasoain Church

q: Baclayon Church in Bohol, built in 1595, holds which distinction?
o: The first all-iron church in the world
The largest church in Metro Manila
The most murals of any church
The oldest church made of stone in the Philippines
n: Baclayon is the oldest church in Bohol and the oldest stone church in the Philippines. Loboc, also in Bohol, is the one with the most murals.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Churches: Baclayon Church

q: What marks Loboc Church's Early Renaissance façade?
n: Loboc's façade has circular windows filling the tympanum. The coconut-tree relief is Miagao's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Loboc Church

q: Who designed the present Baclaran Church, and in what style?
n: Architect César Concio designed Baclaran, the National Shrine of Our Mother of Perpetual Help, in Modern Romanesque. It is the third church on the site.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Baclaran Church

q: What is unusual about Baclaran Church's opening hours since its first mass in 1958?
o: It closes every night at 9 pm
It has been open 24 hours and has never closed
n: Since opening on December 5, 1958 it has stayed open 24 hours, never closing.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Baclaran Church

q: Taal Church in Batangas was started in 1858 by Fray Marcos Anton with which architect?
n: Fray Marcos Anton worked with architect Don Luciano Oliver; the church was completed in 1878.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Taal Church

q: Baguio Cathedral rises above the city skyline in what colour, and how many steps lead up the nearby Lourdes Grotto?
n: Baguio Cathedral has pinkish hues, and the Lourdes Grotto is famous for its 252 steps to heaven.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Baguio Church

q: How is Taal Church approached?
o: It is on top of a hill, reached by flagstone steps
Along a causeway over a lake
Through a walled plaza at street level
By a covered stairway from the river
n: Taal Church is built on a hilltop reached by flagstone steps, unobstructed by other buildings.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Taal Church

q: Why did Baclaran Church take six years to build?
o: Most of the money came from small donations, which often ran out
n: It relied on small donations, the pulpit suggesting 10 centavos per week, and funds often ran out and stopped construction.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Baclaran Church

q: The Franciscans wanted Daraga Church to combine the best of Romanesque and Gothic. In what style did the carvers actually execute it?
n: The carvers executed it in Baroque: a whole-tablet façade without columns or cornices, with whorls, twisted columns, foliage, medallions, statues, and reliefs.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Daraga Church

q: Santo Niño de Cebu was built with stones from where, and its façade blends which styles?
o: Panay and Capiz; Moorish, Romanesque, and Neoclassical
n: It used stones from Panay and Capiz, and its façade blends Moorish, Romanesque, and Neoclassical elements, with trefoils on the doorways.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Niño de Cebu

q: Who began Angat Church in Bulacan (1756–1773), and who completed it in 1802?
o: Fr. Juan de Torres; Fr. Gabriel Sanchez
Augustinian Gregorio Giner; Fray Joaquin Calvo
Fray Marcos Anton; Don Luciano Oliver
n: Gregorio Giner began Angat Church and Fray Joaquin Calvo completed it in 1802.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Angat Church

q: Baclaran Church's foundation stone was laid on January 11, 1953. When was the new church consecrated?
n: It was consecrated December 1, 1958 and opened with a mass on December 5, 1958. October 12, 1954 is Santo Domingo's inauguration.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Baclaran Church

q: Daraga Church in Albay was established by people who fled what?
o: The eruption of Mt. Mayon, from Cagsawa
n: Daraga was founded by people who fled Mt. Mayon's eruption from Cagsawa; the 1814 eruption buried the Cagsawa church, whose belfry ruins still stand.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Daraga Church

q: The belltower of Santo Niño de Cebu is topped by what?
o: A plain balustered top on three storeys
n: Its belltower has a four-sided balustraded dome; inside are pineapple decors at the choir loft and corn cobs at the capitals.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Niño de Cebu

q: Tumauini Church in Isabela was begun in 1783–1788 by whom?
o: Dominican Domingo Forto and town mayor Pablo Sason
n: Dominican Domingo Forto and mayor Pablo Sason began Tumauini; its circular belltower was completed 1803–1808. Gregorio Giner began Angat Church.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Tamauini Church

q: What characterises Taal Church's façade and interior?
o: A whole tablet without columns, covered in whorls and foliage
Arched windows with Ionic columns below and Corinthian above, three pediments, and a cavernous interior of mathematical exactness rather than ornament
Baked-clay reliefs of cherubs and saints
n: Taal has arched windows with Ionic then Corinthian columns and three pediments; inside, stout piers and a semicircular apse show mathematical exactness over ornament.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Taal Church

q: Santo Niño de Cebu was built by Fray Juan de Albarran on the site where a Spanish soldier found what?
o: An image of the Santo Niño in a burned settlement
n: It stands where a soldier found an image of the Santo Niño in a settlement the Spanish had burned down.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Niño de Cebu

q: What makes Tumauini Church unique?
o: Its extensive use of baked clay for both wall finishes and ornament, in an ultra-baroque style
n: Tumauini is ultra-baroque and unique for its extensive baked clay; Pampango artisans carved the hardwood molds for the clay insets.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Tamauini Church

q: Baclaran Church seats how many people, and how many can fit inside including those standing?
n: Baclaran seats 2,000, but as many as 11,000 people can fit inside during masses.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Baclaran Church

q: The convent of Santo Niño de Cebu, founded in 1565, holds which distinction?
o: The first to be built in the country
The first to be declared a UNESCO site
n: Founded in 1565, it was the first convent built in the country.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Niño de Cebu

q: Which church's Baroque façade is divided into levels by coupled Corinthian and Doric columns, beside a plain three-storey belltower with a balustered top?
n: That is Angat Church in Bulacan. Taal uses Ionic below and Corinthian above.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Angat Church

q: The Santo Niño de Cebu church was declared a National Landmark by which president, and what title was conferred on it?
n: Santo Niño de Cebu holds the title Basilica Minore and was declared a National Landmark by President Marcos.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Niño de Cebu

q: Tumauini Church's belltower is distinctive for what?
o: Its separation from the church for earthquake protection
Its circular shape, white limestone finish, and bright red clay rosettes and festoons
Its iron frame shipped from Belgium
n: Tumauini's circular belltower has a white limestone finish decorated with red clay rosettes and festoons. The detached pagoda-like tower is Paoay's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Tamauini Church

q: What role did Miagao Church's two huge, unequal belltowers serve?
o: Watchtowers to defend the town against Moro invasion
n: The belltowers were watchtowers against Moro raids. They differ because two different priests commissioned them; Fr. Francisco Perez added a storey to the east belfry in 1830.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: Miagao Church in Iloilo was declared a National Landmark on what date?
n: Miagao became a National Landmark on August 1, 1973. December 11, 1993 is when Paoay was inscribed as a UNESCO site.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: Which combination appears on Paoay Church's façade?
o: Gothic finials, Chinese elements in the triangular pediment, and Oriental strokes
Twisted columns and statues in niches
A whole tablet without columns or cornices
n: Paoay's façade shows Gothic finials, Chinese elements in the pediment, and Oriental strokes, with brick below and coral above. Coupled Corinthian and Doric columns are Angat's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: Spiral columns run up both storeys of a Baroque front. Which church is it?
n: Quiapo's Baroque façade has twisted columns on both levels. San Agustin uses superposed Tuscan and Corinthian columns instead.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Quiapo Church

q: Paoay's three-storey coral belltower, built in 1793, stands at a distance from the church. Why?
o: Because of a dispute between priests
To make room for a cemetery
n: It stands apart so its fall in an earthquake would not damage the church. It later served as a lookout in 1898 and in World War II.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: What was mixed into the lime mortar of Paoay Church's walls?
o: Sugarcane juice boiled with mango leaves, leather, and rice straw
n: Paoay's sand-and-lime mortar included sugarcane juice boiled with mango leaves, leather, and rice straw. Egg is one of Miagao's materials.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: Miagao's defensive design followed which Spanish colonial law?
o: The Royal Decree of 1565 on convents
Royal Decree 111 of 1573, the Law of the Indies
n: The fortress-like build was stipulated by Royal Decree 111 of 1573, part of the Laws of the Indies. PD 260 declared Paoay a National Cultural Treasure.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: Miagao's massive construction protected the town against Moro invaders. How deep is its foundation and how thick are its stone walls?
n: Miagao's foundation is 6 m deep and its walls 1.5 m thick, reinforced by 4 m thick flying buttresses. 1.67 m is the thickness of Paoay's buttresses.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: How many tons of steel were transported to Manila for San Sebastian Church?
n: 52 tons of steel were shipped to Manila for San Sebastian.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: San Sebastian Church

q: In 1988, Quiapo Church received which title?
o: Basilica Minor de Nuestro Padre Jesus Nazareno
National Shrine of Our Lady of Peace and Good Voyage
n: Quiapo became the Basilica Minor de Nuestro Padre Jesus Nazareno in 1988. Its Baroque façade has twisted columns on both levels.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Quiapo Church

q: San Agustin Church in Manila, designed after the High Renaissance, uses which columns on its two levels?
n: San Agustin superposes Tuscan columns on the first level and Corinthian on the second. Ionic below and Corinthian above is Taal Church.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: San Agustin Church

q: What is the most striking feature of Paoay Church?
o: A ring of 24 massive buttresses, each about 1.67 m deep, bracing its flanks and rear
n: Paoay's 24 massive buttresses, about 1.67 m (5.5 ft) thick, brace it against earthquakes; some are stair-like step buttresses, possibly for roof access.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: Paoay Church in Ilocos Norte is the country's primary example of which style?
n: Paoay is the prime example of 'earthquake baroque', a term dubbed by Alicia Coseteng. Ultra-baroque describes Tumauini.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: What is Miagao Church's overall architectural style, and what gives it its ochre colour?
o: Baroque Romanesque; adobe, egg, coral, and limestone
n: Miagao is Baroque Romanesque, and its ochre colour comes from adobe, egg, coral, and limestone. 'Earthquake Baroque' is the term tied to Paoay.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: Above Miagao's main door is the carved image of which saint, the town's patron?
n: St. Thomas of Villanueva, the patron, is above the door, with St. Henry and Pope Pius VI on either side.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: Paoay Church was declared a National Cultural Treasure by Presidential Decree No. 260 in which year, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site on which date?
n: PD 260 declared Paoay a National Cultural Treasure in 1973, and UNESCO inscribed it on December 11, 1993.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 15–16 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: Miagao Church, officially Santo Tomas de Villanueva Parish Church, is included in which list?
o: The list of Minor Basilicas only
The Seven Wonders of the Philippines
n: Miagao is on the UNESCO World Heritage List, and its façade displays Filipino folk art.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: Paoay Church's walls, of coral stone below and brick above, suggest the influence of which architecture?
n: Javanese architecture reminiscent of Borobudur can be seen on Paoay's walls and façade.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: San Sebastian Church in Manila holds which distinctions?
o: Oldest stone church and oldest in Bohol
First earthquake baroque church and UNESCO site
Largest church in Asia and oldest Marian icon
First all-iron church in the world and first prefabricated structure in the Philippines
n: San Sebastian, made from 52 tons of steel shipped to Manila, is called the first all-iron church in the world and was the first prefabricated structure erected in the Philippines.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: San Sebastian Church

q: Who dubbed the term 'earthquake baroque' for Paoay Church?
n: Alicia Coseteng coined 'earthquake baroque' for Philippine Baroque adapted to seismic conditions.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: Paoay's stair-like buttresses are known as what, and what may they have been for?
o: Step buttresses; easy access to the roof
n: The stair-like step buttresses were possibly meant for easy access to the roof.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Paoay Church

q: What is at the centre of Miagao Church's façade bas-relief?
o: A coconut tree of life held by St. Christopher, in local clothing, carrying the Child Jesus
A galleon and the Virgin of La Naval
The coat of arms of the Augustinians
n: The central coconut tree, a tree of life, is held by St. Christopher dressed in local clothing and carrying the Child Jesus. The relief mixes Medieval Spanish, Chinese, Muslim, and local elements.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 15 — Churches: Miagao Church

q: San Agustin Church in Manila is also known by what name?
n: San Agustin, completed in 1607 and the oldest stone church in Manila, was first dedicated to St. Paul, hence the name Iglesia de San Pablo de Manila. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: San Agustin Church

q: Santo Domingo Church in Quezon City, the largest church in Metro Manila, is the National Shrine of which image?
o: Our Lady of Peace and Good Voyage
Our Lady of the Holy Rosary of La Naval de Manila
n: Santo Domingo is the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary of La Naval de Manila. Our Mother of Perpetual Help is Baclaran's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The sixth and current Santo Domingo Church (1954) in Quezon City was designed by whom?
o: José Ma. Zaragoza, while still an architecture student at UST
n: José Ma. Zaragoza designed it while still a UST student. César Concio designed Baclaran Church.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The fourth Santo Domingo church (1862) had a new façade patterned after which building?
o: London's St. Paul's Cathedral by Christopher Wren
n: Fr. Castro initiated a façade with two towers patterned after Wren's St. Paul's Cathedral; Fr. Francisco Gainza directed the interior. The June 3, 1863 earthquake ruined it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: In what style was the current Santo Domingo Church built?
o: Spanish Modern, in reinforced concrete, with Mission-style Romanesque and Gothic designs
Gótico fingido, in wood and iron
n: The current church is Spanish Modern in reinforced concrete, with Mission-style Romanesque and Gothic elements. Modern Romanesque is Baclaran.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 16–17 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: Who presented the plan for the fifth Santo Domingo church after the 1863 earthquake?
n: European-trained architect Félix Roxas Sr. planned the fifth church. Isabelo Tampinco decorated its interior.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The third Santo Domingo church, rebuilt with a stone vault against fire and earthquake after the fire of 1603, was destroyed when?
n: Despite its stone vault, the third church fell in the earthquake of November 30, 1645, the same quake that ruined Manila Cathedral.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: What distinction does the image of Our Lady of the Rosary of La Naval hold?
o: The only image to survive the 1645 earthquake
The first image brought by Magellan
The oldest Marian icon in the country
n: The La Naval image is the oldest Marian icon in the country and an object of centuries-old devotion.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The fifth Santo Domingo church (1864–1887) was built in 'gótico fingido'. What does that mean?
n: Gótico fingido is a neo-Gothic style; the church used Philippine materials, with columns of acle, molave, and ipil and a vault of zinc or galvanised iron.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The first Santo Domingo church, a small chapel of light materials, was inaugurated on January 1, 1588. Which image was enshrined in it?
o: The Miraculous image of Our Lady of the Rosary from Mexico
Our Lady of Guadalupe from Spain
n: The chapel, erected August 6, 1587, enshrined the Miraculous image of Our Lady of the Rosary from Mexico.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The fourth Santo Domingo church was ruined by the earthquake of which date, one of the strongest in Philippine history?
n: The June 3, 1863 earthquake ruined it; only the high altar remained. August 30, 1864 is when the fifth church's cornerstone was laid.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: Who designed the giant bas-relief of Santo Domingo on the church façade?
n: Francesco Monti, an Italian expatriate sculptor, made the bas-relief. The façade also has a high-relief frieze of the La Naval story.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: After an earthquake partly destroyed the first chapel, the second Santo Domingo church was built of stone under whose direction?
n: Fr. Alonzo Jiménez directed the stone second church, inaugurated April 9, 1592.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: Which National Artist painted the eight murals in the nave on the life of Santo Domingo de Guzmán?
n: Carlos 'Botong' Francisco painted the nave murals. Vicente García Llamas painted the Four Evangelists below them.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: Why did Félix Roxas design the fifth Santo Domingo church with a stone lower storey and a wooden upper storey?
o: To adapt to the seismic realities of Manila
n: Roxas adapted to earthquakes with stone below and wood above, even treating the walls and ceiling to look like stone fan vaults. Isabelo Tampinco carved the interior.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: The current Santo Domingo Church, inaugurated October 12, 1954, has what dimensions?
o: 85 × 40 m, 25 m high, 3,300 sq m of floor area
n: It measures 85 × 40 m and 25 m high, with 3,300 sq m of floor area. 70 × 31 × 22 m is the fifth church.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: After the 1941 bombing, where was the image of Our Lady of the Holy Rosary of La Naval transferred?
o: Santísimo Rosario Church at the University of Santo Tomás
n: The surviving image went to Santísimo Rosario Church at UST in España, Manila.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: How tall did the towers of the fifth Santo Domingo church rise?
n: Its towers rose to 23.3 m. The church measured 70 × 31 × 22 m at the central aisles and 16.6 m high at the lateral aisles.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: On December 21, 1941, the Santo Domingo church in Intramuros was hit by Japanese bombs. What distinction did this give it?
o: The last church rebuilt before independence
The only church to survive the war
The first church to be ruined during the Pacific War
The first church declared a national landmark
n: It was the first church ruined in the Pacific War. San Agustin is the church that survived the war in Intramuros.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 16 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: Who designed the stained-glass windows depicting the 15 Stations of the Holy Rosary at Santo Domingo Church?
n: Galo Ocampo designed the stained glass, which also shows the battles of Lepanto and La Naval de Manila.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 17 — Churches: Santo Domingo Church

q: In the classical Filipino house types, what is a lawig?
n: A lawig is simply a small house. The large house of the Datu is the mala-a-walai.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Lawig

q: How does the torogan's communal kitchen relate to the main house?
o: It is a separate building across a yard
It is under the house at ground level
It is on the roof platform
It is half a metre lower than the main house and used for cooking and eating
n: The kitchen is half a metre below the main house and serves for both cooking and eating.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Architectural Character

q: Which torogan decoration refers to the intricate carvings on the central beams, called the 'intestines' of the house?
n: Tinai-a-walai (or rampatan) are the carved central beams; 'tinai' means intestines.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Decorations

q: What is the torogan used for?
o: As the ancestral house of the datu and family, for social and political ceremonies
n: The torogan is the ornately decorated ancestral house of the datu and his extended family, used for social and political ceremonies. It is the house of the Maranao.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Torogan

q: Why is ventilation an important concern in Maguindanao houses?
o: Because of cooking smoke from indoor hearths
Because of the damp coastal fog
Because of the hot climate on the Cotabato plain
Because of livestock kept under the floor
n: Maguindanao houses sit on the hot Cotabato plain, so ventilation matters. They also have steep roofs and okir decoration.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Mala-a-Walai

q: What is distinctive about the torogan's roof?
o: A tall gable that is narrow at the peak and sweeps outward toward the eaves
A pyramid roof of four equal slopes
A flat roof used as a terrace
A curved barrel vault of bamboo
n: The torogan has a high gable roof, thin at the apex and flaring to the eaves, raised more than 2 m above ground on huge tree trunks set on rock.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Architectural Character

q: On how many posts is a mala-a-walai usually built?
n: It usually stands on nine posts, with a porch linking the house to the kitchen. Twenty-five is the torogan's post count, and four is the Ifugao house.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Mala-a-Walai

q: How was the torogan designed to survive earthquakes?
o: Its posts were buried deep in concrete footings
It was built of heavy stone to resist shaking
It was built to sway, with 25 freestanding tree-trunk posts not buried in the ground
n: Its 25 posts rest freely rather than being buried, so the house sways instead of collapsing; wooden pegs sometimes secure the members.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Architectural Character

q: What are the windows of the torogan like?
o: Slits richly framed in wood panels with okir designs, at the front of the house
Wide openings with bamboo shutters on all sides
n: Torogan windows are slits framed in okir-carved wood panels at the front. Capiz sliding windows belong to later Spanish-era houses.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Architectural Character

q: How is the interior of a mala-a-walai divided?
o: It has four rooms around a central hearth
It has no ceiling and no permanent partitions, only mats, chests, or woven cloths
It has a separate women's wing
It has a ceiling and plank walls between rooms
n: The mala-a-walai is typically one room with no ceiling and no permanent partitions except mats, chests, or woven cloths.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Mala-a-Walai

q: The mala-a-walai, the large house or big house of the Datu, is built of which materials?
n: The mala-a-walai is made of nipa, bamboo, and wood.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Mala-a-Walai

q: In torogan decoration, what is the diongal?
o: The bright cloth hung from the rafters
The carved end beam of the floor
n: Diongal is the apex of the roof. The carved end beam is the panolong.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Decorations

q: What is the panolong?
o: A wing-like beam at the ends of the floor, carved with motifs like the fern or serpent
n: The panolong is the wing-like floor-end beam, carved with pako rabong (fern) or naga (serpent) motifs and painted in bright colours.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Decorations

q: How high is the torogan elevated above the ground?
o: It sits directly on the ground
n: The torogan is raised 0.30 m to 2.20 m and has a single room without partitions. 1.50–2.00 m is the Ifugao house.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Torogan

q: The torogan, the house of kings or royal house, is found in which provinces?
o: Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur
n: The torogan belongs to the Maranao of Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Classical Filipino House: Torogan

q: On a panolong, the motif 'naga' represents what?
n: Naga is the serpent motif; pako rabong is the fern.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Decorations

q: In the torogan, what are malong, hanging from the rafters, meant to signify?
n: Brightly coloured malong weaves hang from the rafters to signify privacy, acting as soft room dividers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Torogan: Decorations

q: In a Badjao community, what connects the houses to each other?
o: Bamboo planks laid out as streets
n: Each house is reached by bamboo planks laid out as streets. Interiors are enclosed by wooden walls nailed permanently for protection.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Badjao House

q: What supports the reed-and-grass roof of the Ifugao house, and how is the house entered?
o: Rafters on the walls; one front door by stairs
Bamboo trusses; a trapdoor in the floor
A brace on a kingpost; two doors on both sides reached by ladder
n: The roof rests on a brace supported by a kingpost, and two doors on both sides are reached by a ladder.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Ifugao House

q: In the bahay kubo, what is the silid?
n: The silid is the private sleeping room.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: A farmer keeps fishing gear, plough tools, and chickens in the space beneath the bahay kubo. What is that space called?
n: The silong is the space under the house used for farm and fishing tools and small animals.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: What is the kamalig?
o: A separate structure for storing rice
n: The kamalig is a separate rice storehouse, apart from the house itself.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: In the bahay kubo, which area is reserved for entertaining guests?
n: The bulwagan receives guests; the silid is the private sleeping room.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: In the bahay kubo kitchen, what is the dapogan?
o: The raised stand holding the river-stone, shoe-shaped stove
n: The dapogan is the raised stand where the shoe-shaped river-stone stove sits. The drying rack for dishes is the banggerahan.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: Which part of the bahay kubo is the kitchen or cooking area?
n: Gilir, or paglutuan, is the kitchen. The kamalig stores rice.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: The trunks used as columns in the Ifugao house come from which tree?
n: Ifugao house trunks come from the amugawan tree. Molave, narra, and yakal are the hardwoods of the bahay na bato.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Ifugao House

q: Badjao houses, on the coast of Tawi-Tawi, are built how?
o: On stilts above shallow water, with bamboo flooring
On coral platforms at the shore
n: Badjao houses stand on stilts over shallow water with bamboo floors.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Badjao House

q: The Ifugao house of the Cordillera mountains has what plan and elevation?
o: Two rooms raised 3.00 m on six posts
A 6.00 m × 8.00 m room raised 0.30 m on nine posts
A single 4.00 m × 6.00 m room raised 1.50–2.00 m on four tree trunks
A circular room at ground level
n: The Ifugao house is a single rectangular room, 4.00 × 6.00 m, lifted 1.50–2.00 m on four tree-trunk columns.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Ifugao House

q: Which material is NOT used for traditional bahay kubo roofing?
n: Bahay kubo roofs use cogon grass, rice stalks, sugar cane leaves, split bamboo, anahaw leaves, or nipa shingles. Clay tiles belong to the bahay na bato.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Nipa Hut / Bahay Kubo

q: Where are pots, pans, glasses, and plates dried and stored in the bahay kubo?
n: The bangahan or banggerahan is the drying and storage place for kitchen utensils.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: The nipa hut, or bahay kubo, is found where, and how did it develop?
o: In lowlands all over the Philippines; it began as one room and grew more sophisticated
Only in the Cordillera; it shrank from a longhouse
Only in Mindanao; it developed from the torogan
On the coast only; it developed from the Badjao house
n: The bahay kubo is a lowland house found across the country; it started as a one-room dwelling and evolved into a more sophisticated type.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Nipa Hut / Bahay Kubo

q: Bahay kubo walls of split bamboo woven in a herringbone pattern are called what?
n: The herringbone-woven bamboo wall is sawali. Anahaw and cogon are roofing materials.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Filipino Architecture: Nipa Hut / Bahay Kubo

q: What is the batalan of a bahay kubo?
o: An unroofed area where water jars are kept
n: The batalan is the unroofed area holding water jars, used for washing.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Kubo

q: Why do very few kotas still stand today?
o: They were destroyed in Spanish campaigns and later American expeditions
They were abandoned after Islam declined
They were dismantled for road materials
They were submerged by rising seas
n: Spanish campaigns dismantled or destroyed most kotas, and American expeditions destroyed many of those rebuilt later.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: The Kota

q: Which Palawan site served as a shelter for the early Filipinos?
n: Tabon Cave in Palawan, where human remains about 47,000 years old were found, sheltered early Filipinos. The Kutawato Cave Complex holds the ruins of Kuta Wato, a later stone fort.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Pre-Historic

q: Besides defence, what other reason did petty chiefs, Datus, and Rajahs have for building forts?
o: Prestige, and to intimidate other chiefs in the area
n: Forts also signalled prestige and intimidated rival chiefs.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Skills in Fortification

q: How did villagers usually enter a Batanes idjang?
o: Through a tunnel from the sea
By a rope ladder that was lowered only for villagers
By stone steps cut into the cliff
n: The only entrance was usually a rope ladder, lowered for villagers and pulled up when invaders came.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Batanes Castles

q: From where did the native Filipinos learn the concept of the kota, or fort?
o: From Muslim scholars arriving from nearby Indonesia
n: The kota came with the arrival of Muslim scholars from nearby Indonesia.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: The Kota

q: Brunei once held a fortified post in Luzon that grew into Manila. What was that kota called?
n: Kota Selurong was the Bruneian outpost that became Manila. Kota Sug is Jolo, in Sulu.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Kota Selurong

q: Besides serving as a military installation, what else was a kota?
o: A palace for the local lord, housing whole families
n: Kotas were occupied by entire families rather than just warriors and served as the local lord's palace as well as a fort.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: The Kota

q: Kota Sug, the seat of the Sultanate of Sulu, was converted by the Spaniards in the 1870s into what?
n: After occupying it in the 1870s, the Spaniards turned the kota in Jolo into the world's smallest walled city.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Kota Sug / Jolo

q: At about what elevation are the Banaue Rice Terraces located, and what feeds them?
o: 1,500 m (5,000 ft), watered by old channels bringing water down from the forest
500 m, fed by the Chico River
n: The terraces sit about 1,500 m (5,000 ft) above sea level and draw water through an ancient irrigation system from the rainforest above.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Banaue Rice Terraces

q: The Banaue Rice Terraces, carved by ancestors of the indigenous people of Ifugao, are about how old?
n: The terraces are about 2,000 years old and are popularly called the "Eighth Wonder of the World".
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Banaue Rice Terraces

q: The Ivatan people of Batanes built hilltop fortifications likened to European castles. What were they called?
n: The Ivatan built idjangs on hills and elevated areas. Kota and moong are the Muslim forts of the south.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Batanes Castles

q: What were kotas usually made of, and what surrounded them?
o: Coral stone, surrounded by moats of seawater
Hardwood logs, surrounded by earth ramparts
Adobe blocks, surrounded by thorny hedges
Stone and bamboo or other light materials, surrounded by trench networks
n: Kotas were built of stone and bamboo or light materials with trench networks around them, which is why many burned easily.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: The Kota

q: The Banaue Rice Terraces are commonly referred to by what title?
o: The Eighth Wonder of the World
The Great Wall of the North
n: They are commonly called the "Eighth Wonder of the World".
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Banaue Rice Terraces

q: What was the first form of man-made dwelling built from indigenous materials?
n: The lean-to came first: a windshield or one-sided shelter, with or without flooring, under a single pitched roof on rafters.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Lean-To

q: What kind of roof did the lean-to have?
o: A hipped roof of cogon grass on a kingpost
A high gable roof flaring to the eaves
A single pitched roof supported by rafters
A flat roof of bamboo slats
n: The lean-to had one pitched roof on rafters. The flaring gable belongs to the torogan, and the kingpost roof to the Ifugao house.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Lean-To

q: The Muslim Filipinos of the south built strong fortresses called what?
n: They built kota or moong, a concept introduced with Muslim scholars from nearby Indonesia. Idjang is the Ivatan fort of Batanes.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: The Kota

q: In the classical period, what first drove early Filipinos to fortify their villages and towns?
o: Wars between neighbouring tribes over territory and trade rights
Orders from the Sultan of Brunei
n: As thalassocratic states made trade flourish, neighbouring tribes fought over territory and trade rights, which led to fortified settlements.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Skills in Fortification

q: At the height of the Maguindanao Sultanate's power, why were kotas spread across Western Mindanao?
o: To block the Spanish advance into the region
To mark the borders with Sulu
n: The Sultanate blanketed Western Mindanao with kotas to stop the Spanish advance.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: The Kota

q: Kuta Wato, or Kota Bato, literally means 'stone fort'. What distinction does it hold?
o: The seat of the Sultanate of Maguindanao's navy
The first known stone fortification in the country
n: Kuta Wato was the first known stone fortification in the country; its ruins are the Kutawato Cave Complex. The smallest walled city is Jolo.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Kuta Wato / Kota Bato

q: The ruins of Kuta Wato survive today under what name?
n: Kuta Wato's ruins exist as the Kutawato Cave Complex.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Kuta Wato / Kota Bato

q: The Igorot forts, built around 2000 BC, had stone walls of what proportions?
o: Several metres wide and about two to three times that width in height
About 1 m wide and 10 m high
As wide as they were high
Thin walls less than 30 cm thick
n: Igorot fort walls averaged several metres in width and rose two to three times their width.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 12 — Filipino Architecture: Igorot Forts

q: A cistern for storing collected rainwater, located underneath the azotea, is called what?
n: The aljibe is the rainwater cistern under the azotea. The batalan is the kubo's water-jar area.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Ground Floor

q: What is the azotea of a bahay na bato?
o: An overhanging balcony facing the street
An open terrace by the toilet, bath, and kitchen, also used for laundry and service
n: The azotea is the open service terrace; the aljibe cistern lies beneath it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: The entresuelo of a bahay na bato is a mezzanine that can only be reached from where?
o: The master's bedroom on the second floor
n: The entresuelo sits over a metre above ground and is accessed only from the master's bedroom upstairs.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Ground Floor

q: In the bahay na bato, what is the caida?
o: The ante-sala, the first room reached from the stairs
n: The caida is the ante-sala, the room you enter first from the ceremonial stairs, before the sala.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: In the bahay na bato, which woods are used as posts supporting the floors, beams, and roof rafters?
n: Molave and ipil serve as posts. Yakal is for floor joists and narra for floor boards.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Spanish Colonial Era: Bahay na Bato

q: How did the bahay na bato separate its sanitary rooms?
o: Toilet and bath shared one room by the sala
Both were on the ground floor by the cuadra
There was no toilet, only a batalan
The comun or latrina was the toilet by the service area, and the banyo or paliguan was a bathroom often built apart from it
n: The comun or latrina is the toilet by the service area; the banyo or paliguan is a bathroom often built separately from the toilet.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: How is the bahay na bato built, compared with the bahay kubo?
o: All stone, replacing the kubo entirely
Stone ground floor and wooden second floor, an improved version of the bahay kubo
n: The bahay na bato, influenced by the Spaniards, has a stone ground floor with a wooden upper floor, improving on the bahay kubo while standing up better to fire and earthquakes.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Spanish Colonial Era: Bahay na Bato

q: Why does the bahay na bato have overhanging eaves around it?
o: To collect rainwater for the aljibe
To shade the zaguan for carriages
To protect the upper storey from the sun's heat and glare and heavy rain
n: The overhanging eaves shield the wooden upper storey from heat, glare, and heavy rain.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Spanish Colonial Era: Bahay na Bato

q: On the ground floor of the bahay na bato, where are carriages and saints' floats kept?
n: The zaguan holds carriages and saints' floats. The cuadra is the horse stable.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Ground Floor

q: What is the balcon of a bahay na bato?
o: The open service terrace at the back
The window seat in the sala
The landing of the main stairs
An overhanging balcony fronting the main street
n: The balcon is the overhanging balcony facing the main street. The back service terrace is the azotea.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: In the bahay na bato, the comedor and the cocina are which rooms?
n: Comedor is the dining room and cocina the kitchen.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: What is the cuadra in a bahay na bato?
n: The cuadra is the horse stable, on the ground floor.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Ground Floor

q: In the bahay na bato, yakal and narra are used for what, respectively?
n: Yakal forms the floor joists and narra the floor boards; molave and ipil are the posts.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Spanish Colonial Era: Bahay na Bato

q: Where in a bahay na bato were balls and dances held during fiestas?
n: The sala is the living room for balls, dances, and other special occasions.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: In the bahay na bato, what is the patio?
o: The front balcony over the street
An enclosed courtyard open to the sky, beside the zaguan
The open terrace by the kitchen
n: The patio is the courtyard open to the sky next to the zaguan. The open terrace by the kitchen is the azotea.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Ground Floor

q: Old furniture and palay bins are stored in which ground-floor room of the bahay na bato?
n: The bodega stores old furniture and palay bins. The dispensa, upstairs, stores food.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 13 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Ground Floor

q: In the bahay na bato, cuarto, alcoba, and dormitorio all name which room?
n: Cuarto, alcoba, and dormitorio all mean bedroom.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: Which room beside the cocina is used for food storage?
n: The dispensa is the food-storage room next to the kitchen. The bodega on the ground floor holds furniture and palay.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Parts of Bahay na Bato: Second Floor

q: Cape Bojeador Lighthouse, a Spanish-era lighthouse at the northern tip of Luzon, stands in which town?
n: Cape Bojeador Lighthouse in Burgos, Ilocos Norte was first lit in 1892 and marks Luzon's northwestern tip. Many lighthouses were built around the islands in the Spanish and American eras.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Lighthouses

q: Of all the buildings in 67-acre Intramuros, which one survived the bombs of World War II?
n: Only San Agustin Church survived. Santo Domingo in Intramuros was destroyed by Japanese bombs in 1941.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Intramuros

q: In what year did the Spaniards erect Fuerza de Santiago, after destroying the native settlement the year before?
n: The conquistadors destroyed Rajah Suliman's settlement in 1570 and built Fuerza de Santiago in 1571.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Fort Santiago

q: Before Fort Santiago, the site held the palace and kingdom of which pre-Spanish ruler?
n: Rajah Suliman, king of Maynila, had his palace there. Lakandula ruled neighbouring Tondo.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Fort Santiago

q: As Paco Park's population of burials grew, what was added, and to whom is its chapel dedicated?
o: An outer wall of thick adobe hollow walls with niches and a walkway on top; St. Pancratius
A second cemetery across the river; St. Augustine
A stone gatehouse; Our Lady of Paco
n: A second outer wall of thick adobe hollow walls with niches was built, its top made into a walkway, and a chapel to St. Pancratius stands inside.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Paco Park

q: Who did the landscape design of Paco Park, from 1967 to 1969?
n: National Artist Ildefonso Santos designed Paco Park's landscape between 1967 and 1969.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Paco Park

q: Intramuros, the old walled city of Manila, lies along which bank of the Pasig River?
o: On an island in the river
n: Intramuros is on the southern bank of the Pasig River.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Intramuros

q: Fort Santiago (Fuerza de Santiago), the citadel of Intramuros, was established by which Spanish conquistador?
n: Miguel López de Legazpi established Fort Santiago.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Fort Santiago

q: Paco Park was originally planned as what?
o: A municipal cemetery for well-off Spanish families of Intramuros
n: Paco Park began as a circular cemetery for aristocratic Spanish families; its original inner circular fort had niches in its hollow walls.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 14 — Spanish Colonial Era: Paco Park
